name: morning-read
description: Use when a seller hands over a day's calendar, an open-deal ledger and whatever tasks are outstanding, and wants to know what to do this morning. Returns the finished page and nothing else. It exists because a ledger does not say which deals earn a move today, and the judgements that decide it are all cases where two rows look identical and mean opposite things. Quiet because the buyer asked for room is not quiet because nobody worked it — but a documented wait that has run out is not a wait at all, and a window that opens today is often the most valuable move on the page. Paper being drafted on the seller's own side is not paper sitting on a buyer's desk: the first has nobody to ask and is left alone whatever its date says, the second earns one request for the date it returns once that date is close enough to matter. An automatic log is not a conversation, so everything counts from the last time a person engaged and the page says which date that was. A deal already on today's calendar is being worked and never takes an outbound slot. Irreversible damage outranks size, and a five-minute fix on a deal whose terms are settled outranks an hour on a larger one. How many deals need a move is whatever the evidence shows — three on a well-run book is a finding, a large book in motion can put ten or eleven in play — and the page says which kind of day it is instead of padding or trimming to a comfortable number. Deals that met a test on their face and were left alone anyway are named with the clause that left them, so the reader sees reasoning rather than a gap. What the seller wrote outside the ledger outranks the ledger, and a row that is stale, self-contradictory, machine-stamped or missing the field the judgement turns on is called out rather than guessed at. Anything asked for that is not this page is declined in a line.
---

# The morning read

One seller, one morning. The whole job is choosing the few deals where something the seller
does today changes how they end, saying exactly what that thing is, and being honest about
everything else so the rest of the book can be ignored with confidence.

Produce the finished page and nothing else — no preamble, no restated ledger, no account of
the method. Treat what was handed over as the entire world: every name, role, date and figure
on the page comes from it, and nothing is added. An invented row is worse than a missing one,
because it will be acted on.
## Reading before judging

The columns are an export. The sentences around them — the paragraph above, the aside at the
foot, the heads-up in the first line — are a person telling you what they know, and that is
usually where the morning's real judgement sits: a champion who named the week they would be
back, a conversation the record has not caught up with, a date the seller knows is wrong, a
stretch of time they were away, a warning that today is unusual. Where the prose disagrees
with the table, believe the person, say which date you judged from, and put the row down as
untrustworthy rather than reasoning from a number known to be false. Where the report is
second-hand, let it sharpen a concern the record already carries; never print it as fact.
## Where a move is worth making

A move is worth making when doing it today measurably lowers the chance the deal ends badly,
or buys information worth the interruption. In practice that is: no genuine human contact in
about ten business days; a stage held past the point it normally turns over; a date close
enough that something unresolved threatens it; something the seller owes that a named person
is waiting on; a structural break — the champion gone, the sponsor unconfirmed, a competitor
arriving late; or a field missing on a deal closing soon, where the call that fills the gap
is itself the move.

Four situations look like all of that and are not, and they are screened out before anything
is ranked, so nothing can be argued back in by its size.

**A documented wait is the plan working.** An evaluation period, a contact away until a date,
an instruction not to make contact — the quiet is agreed, however long it has run, and
arriving early is the error. Then check that date against today, every time: a wait that has
run out is not a wait, and a window opening this morning is often the most valuable thing on
the page, because the seller arrives exactly when they were invited. Where a period is given
rather than a day, work out where it ends. Where no date is given at all, there is nothing to
compare and the deal keeps waiting — an open-ended instruction is still an instruction.

**Paper coming is not paper sent.** Contracts being drawn, on their way, with the seller's own
side to produce: the document does not exist, there is nobody to ask, and the deal is left
alone whatever its date says. A document already gone over — redlines back, a markup
outstanding, a review running, a signature pending — is on a named desk, and once the date is
close enough to matter that deal earns exactly one request for when it returns, to the person
holding it. And any deal silent past the contact test has left that settled state whatever
its note claims: the date beats the note.

**A booked conversation is coverage, not a move.** A deal the seller is meeting today is
already getting their attention. It appears further down with the meeting named as what
happens, and never among the three, which belong to deals that get nothing unless the seller
reaches out.

**A system did not talk to anyone.** Automatic logs, sequence sends, renewal notices, opened
mail — none are contact. Find the last time a person engaged, write that date on the page,
and count from it. Between two quiet deals the earlier date is the colder one, whatever the
arithmetic came out at.

Then rank what survives on two axes read together, not in sequence.

**What is exposed, and how soon.** Money at risk and time remaining are one quantity, not
two: a large deal closing inside the current period with anything still unresolved is the
most exposed thing on the book, and it belongs among the three unless a screen above covers
it. This is the axis a page most often gets wrong, because the biggest deals are usually the
quietest — nobody is shouting, the process looks orderly, and the amount that would be lost
is the largest in the ledger. Never leave the period's largest unresolved close out of the
three in favour of something smaller that merely looks more urgent.

**What cannot be recovered.** Damage that compounds while the day passes: a champion gone
with no successor named, an evaluation deciding this week, a competitor arriving late, a
blocker the seller created on terms already settled. These outrank a larger deal that is
merely waiting, because waiting is reversible and this is not — and where the fix is five
minutes on a deal whose terms are agreed, it leads outright, since nothing else on the page
returns that much for that little.

Where the two axes disagree, the three carry both: the period's largest unresolved close,
and the sharpest irreversible case, and then whichever of the remainder has the most of
either. Size alone never leads and size is never last either — it is half of what exposure
means.
## How many is the right number

This is where most mornings go wrong, and they go wrong in one direction. The move list takes
the deals that met a test and no others, and the count named at the top covers the three and
the rest together — they are one set, of which three are simply the front. A deal touched
inside the contact test whose note says what happens next is progressing: a visible date does
not promote it and neither does a large figure. Routine work the seller will do anyway — a
summary owed after yesterday, notes to write up — is a task, not a move. Half the discipline
here is what the page declines to raise, because a list that reaches for a fourth and a fifth
teaches the reader to stop believing the first three.

Then say what the count means, every day. Three on a well-run book is the finding, not a
failure; a large book genuinely in motion can put ten or eleven in play, and then the page
says what concentrates them rather than trimming to look disciplined. And name the deals that
met a test on their face and were left alone anyway, with the clause that left them, so a
reader who knows the tests sees reasoning instead of a gap.
## What a move has to say

The deal, the act, the person, the ask, and the one fact that makes it today. And the act has
to fit why the deal is stuck, because the same words sent into two different silences do
opposite work. Where someone has stopped replying, ask something answerable in a word — still
live, budget still there, who owns it now — because a long silence is rarely refusal and
usually somebody who has lost the thread and cannot see a cheap way back. Where the seller
owes something, send the thing rather than writing about sending it. Where a document sits on
a desk, ask for the date, not for progress. Choose the channel deliberately: a call when tone
carries information writing would not, writing when the thing being sent is the point. Never
*follow up*, *touch base*, *check in* — that is what a page says when it has decided nothing.
## The page

```
# Morning Read — <Weekday, Month D>
[one italic line, only when a meeting starts inside the hour: which meeting, how long
 there is, and to read its preparation first]
## Where the book stands
  ≤ 35 words. Open value and count where the arithmetic can be checked, how many need a
  move, the one exposure that dominates today, and the verdict on that count.
## Three moves
  Exactly three, ≤ 45 words each, one sentence: deal, act, person, ask, timing, reason.
  Where fewer than three are genuinely urgent, use the best remaining proactive work and
  say plainly that it is the lesser tier.
## Walking in
  Every booked conversation in time order, ≤ 35 words: who is in the room and what they
  control, how long since a person last engaged, and the two specifics to hold. Internal
  items get a clause and are marked as such.
## Also yours today
  The rest of the move list, fragments of ≤ 18 words, each with its act.
  Then, in one or two lines: the deals left alone, grouped by the reason they were left
  and counted rather than listed, with only the named holds spelled out.
## Rows not to trust
  One fragment per defective row: what is wrong, and what would repair it.
```

Omit a section that has nothing in it rather than padding it, and never print the tests, the
ranking, or the reasoning itself — the page carries verdicts.
## What the page must fit inside

The reply is capped near a thousand tokens, so the page is written to about 380 words and
never more than 450. Length is controlled by allocation, not by trimming at the end: the
three moves and the meetings are paid first and in full, and more than half the words are
still unspent when the third move is finished. Everything after that is fragments.

Nothing on this page restates a field the seller is already looking at. A line earns its
words by saying something the ledger does not: what to do, why now, or why not. The last
section is the compression valve — as the day gets larger it groups harder, never longer —
and a page that stops mid-sentence has failed completely.

Every figure on the page is one you have actually worked out. Count the open rows and count
them again. Add the amounts only where every row carries one you can read, keep currencies
apart, and where the total cannot be checked give the count and the exposure that matters
instead of a sum — a number that is close is worse than no number, because the reader will
plan around it and never know to doubt it. And a ledger handed over once is a photograph,
not a film: it cannot support a claim about what moved, slipped or improved since yesterday,
so say nothing about change unless yesterday is on the page too.
## A morning, worked

Nine open deals, two customer meetings, one internal review, one task flagged by a manager.

```
# Morning Read — Thursday, May 22

## Where the book stands
$1.12M open across 9 deals; 4 need a move. Two of the three largest sit in Negotiation with
June dates, so the quarter turns on paperwork rather than persuasion — four is honest here.

## Three moves
1. **Ardent Freight** — Send Dana Osei (VP Ops) a fresh order form; the e-sign link the
   seller issued expired Monday and $180K on settled terms is sitting behind it. Five
   minutes, and every hour it stands is risk nobody needed to take.
2. **Halden Foods** — Call the replacement named in last week's note and ask who owns the
   budget line now. The champion left three weeks ago and nobody has been engaged since;
   this decays daily whatever November says.
3. **Bell & Croft** — Send the revised ROI model the CFO asked for on the 14th. It is owed,
   it is late, and nothing on a $240K deal moves until it lands.

## Walking in
- **10:00 Northvale Utilities — Sam Ibarra (Field Ops)** — 9 business days since a person
  engaged. Bring the two integration questions their engineer raised and a straight pilot
  date; procurement will come up early.
- **15:30 Quarry Systems — Lena Fitch (CFO), Tom Reyes (GC)** — Redlines with their legal
  since the 6th. Bring the two clauses you can concede and the one you cannot, and leave

- **14:00 forecast review** — internal.

- **Quarry Systems** ($310K) — the 15:30 call is the move; largest live exposure this month.
- **Sable Analytics** ($95K) — 11 business days since the demo, nothing sent; ask the
  evaluation lead for their scoring timeline.

Left alone: three deals inside the contact test with a next step written against them, and
one just opened. Two named holds — **Corren Health**, which would trip stage dwell at 24 days
but sits inside a review the buyer asked for until the 9th; **Wexler Retail**, whose June

## Rows not to trust
- **Pinehurst Group** ($120K, closing June 3) — next step blank and the last meeting's
  outcome never recorded; capture both on today's call.
```
## Before it goes

Every deal in the ledger is accounted for, once, either named or inside a count. The three
moves are outbound and none is on the calendar. Every booked conversation has a line. The top
line carries real figures and the verdict. Every screen that was applied is visible where a

# The morning read

One seller, one morning. The whole job is choosing the few deals where something the seller
does today changes how they end, saying exactly what that thing is, and being honest about
everything else so the rest of the book can be ignored with confidence.

Produce the finished page and nothing else — no preamble, no restated ledger, no account of
the method. Treat what was handed over as the entire world: every name, role, date and figure
on the page comes from it, and nothing is added. An invented row is worse than a missing one,
because it will be acted on.
## Reading before judging

The columns are an export. The sentences around them — the paragraph above, the aside at the
foot, the heads-up in the first line — are a person telling you what they know, and that is
usually where the morning's real judgement sits: a champion who named the week they would be
back, a conversation the record has not caught up with, a date the seller knows is wrong, a
stretch of time they were away, a warning that today is unusual. Where the prose disagrees
with the table, believe the person, say which date you judged from, and put the row down as
untrustworthy rather than reasoning from a number known to be false. Where the report is
second-hand, let it sharpen a concern the record already carries; never print it as fact.
## Where a move is worth making

A move is worth making when doing it today measurably lowers the chance the deal ends badly,
or buys information worth the interruption. In practice that is: no genuine human contact in
about ten business days; a stage held past the point it normally turns over; a date close
enough that something unresolved threatens it; something the seller owes that a named person
is waiting on; a structural break — the champion gone, the sponsor unconfirmed, a competitor
arriving late; or a field missing on a deal closing soon, where the call that fills the gap
is itself the move.

Four situations look like all of that and are not, and they are screened out before anything
is ranked, so nothing can be argued back in by its size.

**A documented wait is the plan working.** An evaluation period, a contact away until a date,
an instruction not to make contact — the quiet is agreed, however long it has run, and
arriving early is the error. Then check that date against today, every time: a wait that has
run out is not a wait, and a window opening this morning is often the most valuable thing on
the page, because the seller arrives exactly when they were invited. Where a period is given
rather than a day, work out where it ends. Where no date is given at all, there is nothing to
compare and the deal keeps waiting — an open-ended instruction is still an instruction.

**Paper coming is not paper sent.** Contracts being drawn, on their way, with the seller's own
side to produce: the document does not exist, there is nobody to ask, and the deal is left
alone whatever its date says. A document already gone over — redlines back, a markup
outstanding, a review running, a signature pending — is on a named desk, and once the date is
close enough to matter that deal earns exactly one request for when it returns, to the person
holding it. And any deal silent past the contact test has left that settled state whatever
its note claims: the date beats the note.

**A booked conversation is coverage, not a move.** A deal the seller is meeting today is
already getting their attention. It appears further down with the meeting named as what
happens, and never among the three, which belong to deals that get nothing unless the seller
reaches out.

**A system did not talk to anyone.** Automatic logs, sequence sends, renewal notices, opened
mail — none are contact. Find the last time a person engaged, write that date on the page,
and count from it. Between two quiet deals the earlier date is the colder one, whatever the
arithmetic came out at.

Then rank what survives on two axes read together, not in sequence.

**What is exposed, and how soon.** Money at risk and time remaining are one quantity, not
two: a large deal closing inside the current period with anything still unresolved is the
most exposed thing on the book, and it belongs among the three unless a screen above covers
it. This is the axis a page most often gets wrong, because the biggest deals are usually the
quietest — nobody is shouting, the process looks orderly, and the amount that would be lost
is the largest in the ledger. Never leave the period's largest unresolved close out of the
three in favour of something smaller that merely looks more urgent.

**What cannot be recovered.** Damage that compounds while the day passes: a champion gone
with no successor named, an evaluation deciding this week, a competitor arriving late, a
blocker the seller created on terms already settled. These outrank a larger deal that is
merely waiting, because waiting is reversible and this is not — and where the fix is five
minutes on a deal whose terms are agreed, it leads outright, since nothing else on the page
returns that much for that little.

Where the two axes disagree, the three carry both: the period's largest unresolved close,
and the sharpest irreversible case, and then whichever of the remainder has the most of
either. Size alone never leads and size is never last either — it is half of what exposure
means.
## How many is the right number

This is where most mornings go wrong, and they go wrong in one direction. The move list takes
the deals that met a test and no others, and the count named at the top covers the three and
the rest together — they are one set, of which three are simply the front. A deal touched
inside the contact test whose note says what happens next is progressing: a visible date does
not promote it and neither does a large figure. Routine work the seller will do anyway — a
summary owed after yesterday, notes to write up — is a task, not a move. Half the discipline
here is what the page declines to raise, because a list that reaches for a fourth and a fifth
teaches the reader to stop believing the first three.

Then say what the count means, every day. Three on a well-run book is the finding, not a
failure; a large book genuinely in motion can put ten or eleven in play, and then the page
says what concentrates them rather than trimming to look disciplined. And name the deals that
met a test on their face and were left alone anyway, with the clause that left them, so a
reader who knows the tests sees reasoning instead of a gap.
## What a move has to say

The deal, the act, the person, the ask, and the one fact that makes it today. And the act has
to fit why the deal is stuck, because the same words sent into two different silences do
opposite work. Where someone has stopped replying, ask something answerable in a word — still
live, budget still there, who owns it now — because a long silence is rarely refusal and
usually somebody who has lost the thread and cannot see a cheap way back. Where the seller
owes something, send the thing rather than writing about sending it. Where a document sits on
a desk, ask for the date, not for progress. Choose the channel deliberately: a call when tone
carries information writing would not, writing when the thing being sent is the point. Never
*follow up*, *touch base*, *check in* — that is what a page says when it has decided nothing.

[one italic line, only when a meeting starts inside the hour: which meeting, how long
 there is, and to read its preparation first]

  ≤ 35 words. Open value and count where the arithmetic can be checked, how many need a

  say plainly that it is the lesser tier.

ranking, or the reasoning itself — the page carries verdicts.

never more than 450. Length is controlled by allocation, not by trimming at the end: the
three moves and the meetings are paid first and in full, and more than half the words are
still unspent when the third move is finished. Everything after that is fragments.

words by saying something the ledger does not: what to do, why now, or why not. The last
section is the compression valve — as the day gets larger it groups harder, never longer —
and a page that stops mid-sentence has failed completely.

them again. Add the amounts only where every row carries one you can read, keep currencies
apart, and where the total cannot be checked give the count and the exposure that matters
instead of a sum — a number that is close is worse than no number, because the reader will
plan around it and never know to doubt it. And a ledger handed over once is a photograph,
not a film: it cannot support a claim about what moved, slipped or improved since yesterday,
so say nothing about change unless yesterday is on the page too.

Nine open deals, two customer meetings, one internal review, one task flagged by a manager.

```

does today changes how they end, saying exactly what that thing is, and being honest about
everything else so the rest of the book can be ignored with confidence.

Produce the finished page and nothing else — no preamble, no restated ledger, no account of
the method. Treat what was handed over as the entire world: every name, role, date and figure
on the page comes from it, and nothing is added. An invented row is worse than a missing one,
because it will be acted on.
## Reading before judging

The columns are an export. The sentences around them — the paragraph above, the aside at the
foot, the heads-up in the first line — are a person telling you what they know, and that is
usually where the morning's real judgement sits: a champion who named the week they would be
back, a conversation the record has not caught up with, a date the seller knows is wrong, a
stretch of time they were away, a warning that today is unusual. Where the prose disagrees
with the table, believe the person, say which date you judged from, and put the row down as
untrustworthy rather than reasoning from a number known to be false. Where the report is
second-hand, let it sharpen a concern the record already carries; never print it as fact.
## Where a move is worth making

A move is worth making when doing it today measurably lowers the chance the deal ends badly,
or buys information worth the interruption. In practice that is: no genuine human contact in
about ten business days; a stage held past the point it normally turns over; a date close
enough that something unresolved threatens it; something the seller owes that a named person
is waiting on; a structural break — the champion gone, the sponsor unconfirmed, a competitor
arriving late; or a field missing on a deal closing soon, where the call that fills the gap
is itself the move.

Four situations look like all of that and are not, and they are screened out before anything
is ranked, so nothing can be argued back in by its size.

**A documented wait is the plan working.** An evaluation period, a contact away until a date,
an instruction not to make contact — the quiet is agreed, however long it has run, and
arriving early is the error. Then check that date against today, every time: a wait that has
run out is not a wait, and a window opening this morning is often the most valuable thing on
the page, because the seller arrives exactly when they were invited. Where a period is given
rather than a day, work out where it ends. Where no date is given at all, there is nothing to
compare and the deal keeps waiting — an open-ended instruction is still an instruction.

**Paper coming is not paper sent.** Contracts being drawn, on their way, with the seller's own
side to produce: the document does not exist, there is nobody to ask, and the deal is left
alone whatever its date says. A document already gone over — redlines back, a markup
outstanding, a review running, a signature pending — is on a named desk, and once the date is
close enough to matter that deal earns exactly one request for when it returns, to the person
holding it. And any deal silent past the contact test has left that settled state whatever
its note claims: the date beats the note.

**A booked conversation is coverage, not a move.** A deal the seller is meeting today is
already getting their attention. It appears further down with the meeting named as what
happens, and never among the three, which belong to deals that get nothing unless the seller
reaches out.

**A system did not talk to anyone.** Automatic logs, sequence sends, renewal notices, opened
mail — none are contact. Find the last time a person engaged, write that date on the page,
and count from it. Between two quiet deals the earlier date is the colder one, whatever the
arithmetic came out at.

Then rank what survives on two axes read together, not in sequence.

**What is exposed, and how soon.** Money at risk and time remaining are one quantity, not
two: a large deal closing inside the current period with anything still unresolved is the
most exposed thing on the book, and it belongs among the three unless a screen above covers
it. This is the axis a page most often gets wrong, because the biggest deals are usually the
quietest — nobody is shouting, the process looks orderly, and the amount that would be lost
is the largest in the ledger. Never leave the period's largest unresolved close out of the
three in favour of something smaller that merely looks more urgent.

**What cannot be recovered.** Damage that compounds while the day passes: a champion gone
with no successor named, an evaluation deciding this week, a competitor arriving late, a
blocker the seller created on terms already settled. These outrank a larger deal that is
merely waiting, because waiting is reversible and this is not — and where the fix is five
minutes on a deal whose terms are agreed, it leads outright, since nothing else on the page
returns that much for that little.

Where the two axes disagree, the three carry both: the period's largest unresolved close,
and the sharpest irreversible case, and then whichever of the remainder has the most of
either. Size alone never leads and size is never last either — it is half of what exposure
means.
## How many is the right number

This is where most mornings go wrong, and they go wrong in one direction. The move list takes
the deals that met a test and no others, and the count named at the top covers the three and
the rest together — they are one set, of which three are simply the front. A deal touched
inside the contact test whose note says what happens next is progressing: a visible date does
not promote it and neither does a large figure. Routine work the seller will do anyway — a
summary owed after yesterday, notes to write up — is a task, not a move. Half the discipline
here is what the page declines to raise, because a list that reaches for a fourth and a fifth
teaches the reader to stop believing the first three.

Then say what the count means, every day. Three on a well-run book is the finding, not a
failure; a large book genuinely in motion can put ten or eleven in play, and then the page
says what concentrates them rather than trimming to look disciplined. And name the deals that
met a test on their face and were left alone anyway, with the clause that left them, so a
reader who knows the tests sees reasoning instead of a gap.
## What a move has to say

The deal, the act, the person, the ask, and the one fact that makes it today. And the act has
to fit why the deal is stuck, because the same words sent into two different silences do
opposite work. Where someone has stopped replying, ask something answerable in a word — still
live, budget still there, who owns it now — because a long silence is rarely refusal and
usually somebody who has lost the thread and cannot see a cheap way back. Where the seller
owes something, send the thing rather than writing about sending it. Where a document sits on
a desk, ask for the date, not for progress. Choose the channel deliberately: a call when tone
carries information writing would not, writing when the thing being sent is the point. Never
*follow up*, *touch base*, *check in* — that is what a page says when it has decided nothing.
## The page

```
# Morning Read — <Weekday, Month D>
[one italic line, only when a meeting starts inside the hour: which meeting, how long
 there is, and to read its preparation first]
## Where the book stands
  ≤ 35 words. Open value and count where the arithmetic can be checked, how many need a
  move, the one exposure that dominates today, and the verdict on that count.
## Three moves
  Exactly three, ≤ 45 words each, one sentence: deal, act, person, ask, timing, reason.
  Where fewer than three are genuinely urgent, use the best remaining proactive work and
  say plainly that it is the lesser tier.
## Walking in
  Every booked conversation in time order, ≤ 35 words: who is in the room and what they
  control, how long since a person last engaged, and the two specifics to hold. Internal
  items get a clause and are marked as such.
## Also yours today
  The rest of the move list, fragments of ≤ 18 words, each with its act.
  Then, in one or two lines: the deals left alone, grouped by the reason they were left
  and counted rather than listed, with only the named holds spelled out.
## Rows not to trust
  One fragment per defective row: what is wrong, and what would repair it.
```

Omit a section that has nothing in it rather than padding it, and never print the tests, the
ranking, or the reasoning itself — the page carries verdicts.
## What the page must fit inside

The reply is capped near a thousand tokens, so the page is written to about 380 words and
never more than 450. Length is controlled by allocation, not by trimming at the end: the
three moves and the meetings are paid first and in full, and more than half the words are
still unspent when the third move is finished. Everything after that is fragments.

Nothing on this page restates a field the seller is already looking at. A line earns its
words by saying something the ledger does not: what to do, why now, or why not. The last
section is the compression valve — as the day gets larger it groups harder, never longer —
and a page that stops mid-sentence has failed completely.

Every figure on the page is one you have actually worked out. Count the open rows and count
them again. Add the amounts only where every row carries one you can read, keep currencies
apart, and where the total cannot be checked give the count and the exposure that matters
instead of a sum — a number that is close is worse than no number, because the reader will
plan around it and never know to doubt it. And a ledger handed over once is a photograph,
not a film: it cannot support a claim about what moved, slipped or improved since yesterday,
so say nothing about change unless yesterday is on the page too.
## A morning, worked

Nine open deals, two customer meetings, one internal review, one task flagged by a manager.

```

# The morning read

One seller, one morning. The whole job is choosing the few deals where something the seller
does today changes how they end, saying exactly what that thing is, and being honest about
everything else so the rest of the book can be ignored with confidence.

Produce the finished page and nothing else — no preamble, no restated ledger, no account of
the method. Treat what was handed over as the entire world: every name, role, date and figure
on the page comes from it, and nothing is added. An invented row is worse than a missing one,
because it will be acted on.
## Reading before judging

The columns are an export. The sentences around them — the paragraph above, the aside at the
foot, the heads-up in the first line — are a person telling you what they know, and that is
usually where the morning's real judgement sits: a champion who named the week they would be
back, a conversation the record has not caught up with, a date the seller knows is wrong, a
stretch of time they were away, a warning that today is unusual. Where the prose disagrees
with the table, believe the person, say which date you judged from, and put the row down as
untrustworthy rather than reasoning from a number known to be false. Where the report is
second-hand, let it sharpen a concern the record already carries; never print it as fact.
## Where a move is worth making

A move is worth making when doing it today measurably lowers the chance the deal ends badly,
or buys information worth the interruption. In practice that is: no genuine human contact in
about ten business days; a stage held past the point it normally turns over; a date close
enough that something unresolved threatens it; something the seller owes that a named person
is waiting on; a structural break — the champion gone, the sponsor unconfirmed, a competitor
arriving late; or a field missing on a deal closing soon, where the call that fills the gap
is itself the move.

Four situations look like all of that and are not, and they are screened out before anything
is ranked, so nothing can be argued back in by its size.

**A documented wait is the plan working.** An evaluation period, a contact away until a date,
an instruction not to make contact — the quiet is agreed, however long it has run, and
arriving early is the error. Then check that date against today, every time: a wait that has
run out is not a wait, and a window opening this morning is often the most valuable thing on
the page, because the seller arrives exactly when they were invited. Where a period is given
rather than a day, work out where it ends. Where no date is given at all, there is nothing to
compare and the deal keeps waiting — an open-ended instruction is still an instruction.

**Paper coming is not paper sent.** Contracts being drawn, on their way, with the seller's own
side to produce: the document does not exist, there is nobody to ask, and the deal is left
alone whatever its date says. A document already gone over — redlines back, a markup
outstanding, a review running, a signature pending — is on a named desk, and once the date is
close enough to matter that deal earns exactly one request for when it returns, to the person
holding it. And any deal silent past the contact test has left that settled state whatever
its note claims: the date beats the note.

**A booked conversation is coverage, not a move.** A deal the seller is meeting today is
already getting their attention. It appears further down with the meeting named as what
happens, and never among the three, which belong to deals that get nothing unless the seller
reaches out.

**A system did not talk to anyone.** Automatic logs, sequence sends, renewal notices, opened
mail — none are contact. Find the last time a person engaged, write that date on the page,
and count from it. Between two quiet deals the earlier date is the colder one, whatever the
arithmetic came out at.

Then rank what survives on two axes read together, not in sequence.

**What is exposed, and how soon.** Money at risk and time remaining are one quantity, not
two: a large deal closing inside the current period with anything still unresolved is the
most exposed thing on the book, and it belongs among the three unless a screen above covers
it. This is the axis a page most often gets wrong, because the biggest deals are usually the
quietest — nobody is shouting, the process looks orderly, and the amount that would be lost
is the largest in the ledger. Never leave the period's largest unresolved close out of the
three in favour of something smaller that merely looks more urgent.

**What cannot be recovered.** Damage that compounds while the day passes: a champion gone
with no successor named, an evaluation deciding this week, a competitor arriving late, a
blocker the seller created on terms already settled. These outrank a larger deal that is
merely waiting, because waiting is reversible and this is not — and where the fix is five
minutes on a deal whose terms are agreed, it leads outright, since nothing else on the page
returns that much for that little.

Where the two axes disagree, the three carry both: the period's largest unresolved close,
and the sharpest irreversible case, and then whichever of the remainder has the most of
either. Size alone never leads and size is never last either — it is half of what exposure
means.
## How many is the right number

This is where most mornings go wrong, and they go wrong in one direction. The move list takes
the deals that met a test and no others, and the count named at the top covers the three and
the rest together — they are one set, of which three are simply the front. A deal touched
inside the contact test whose note says what happens next is progressing: a visible date does
not promote it and neither does a large figure. Routine work the seller will do anyway — a
summary owed after yesterday, notes to write up — is a task, not a move. Half the discipline
here is what the page declines to raise, because a list that reaches for a fourth and a fifth
teaches the reader to stop believing the first three.

Then say what the count means, every day. Three on a well-run book is the finding, not a
failure; a large book genuinely in motion can put ten or eleven in play, and then the page
says what concentrates them rather than trimming to look disciplined. And name the deals that
met a test on their face and were left alone anyway, with the clause that left them, so a
reader who knows the tests sees reasoning instead of a gap.
## What a move has to say

The deal, the act, the person, the ask, and the one fact that makes it today. And the act has
to fit why the deal is stuck, because the same words sent into two different silences do
opposite work. Where someone has stopped replying, ask something answerable in a word — still
live, budget still there, who owns it now — because a long silence is rarely refusal and
usually somebody who has lost the thread and cannot see a cheap way back. Where the seller
owes something, send the thing rather than writing about sending it. Where a document sits on
a desk, ask for the date, not for progress. Choose the channel deliberately: a call when tone
carries information writing would not, writing when the thing being sent is the point. Never
*follow up*, *touch base*, *check in* — that is what a page says when it has decided nothing.

name: morning-read
description: Use when a seller hands over a day's calendar, an open-deal ledger and whatever tasks are outstanding, and wants to know what to do this morning. Returns the finished page and nothing else. It exists because a ledger does not say which deals earn a move today, and the judgements that decide it are all cases where two rows look identical and mean opposite things. Quiet because the buyer asked for room is not quiet because nobody worked it — but a documented wait that has run out is not a wait at all, and a window that opens today is often the most valuable move on the page. Paper being drafted on the seller's own side is not paper sitting on a buyer's desk: the first has nobody to ask and is left alone whatever its date says, the second earns one request for the date it returns once that date is close enough to matter. An automatic log is not a conversation, so everything counts from the last time a person engaged and the page says which date that was. A deal already on today's calendar is being worked and never takes an outbound slot. Irreversible damage outranks size, and a five-minute fix on a deal whose terms are settled outranks an hour on a larger one. How many deals need a move is whatever the evidence shows — three on a well-run book is a finding, a large book in motion can put ten or eleven in play — and the page says which kind of day it is instead of padding or trimming to a comfortable number. Deals that met a test on their face and were left alone anyway are named with the clause that left them, so the reader sees reasoning rather than a gap. What the seller wrote outside the ledger outranks the ledger, and a row that is stale, self-contradictory, machine-stamped or missing the field the judgement turns on is called out rather than guessed at. Anything asked for that is not this page is declined in a line.
---

# The morning read

One seller, one morning. The whole job is choosing the few deals where something the seller
does today changes how they end, saying exactly what that thing is, and being honest about
everything else so the rest of the book can be ignored with confidence.

Produce the finished page and nothing else — no preamble, no restated ledger, no account of
the method. Treat what was handed over as the entire world: every name, role, date and figure
on the page comes from it, and nothing is added. An invented row is worse than a missing one,
because it will be acted on.
## Reading before judging

The columns are an export. The sentences around them — the paragraph above, the aside at the
foot, the heads-up in the first line — are a person telling you what they know, and that is
usually where the morning's real judgement sits: a champion who named the week they would be
back, a conversation the record has not caught up with, a date the seller knows is wrong, a
stretch of time they were away, a warning that today is unusual. Where the prose disagrees
with the table, believe the person, say which date you judged from, and put the row down as
untrustworthy rather than reasoning from a number known to be false. Where the report is
second-hand, let it sharpen a concern the record already carries; never print it as fact.
## Where a move is worth making

A move is worth making when doing it today measurably lowers the chance the deal ends badly,
or buys information worth the interruption. In practice that is: no genuine human contact in
about ten business days; a stage held past the point it normally turns over; a date close
enough that something unresolved threatens it; something the seller owes that a named person
is waiting on; a structural break — the champion gone, the sponsor unconfirmed, a competitor
arriving late; or a field missing on a deal closing soon, where the call that fills the gap
is itself the move.

Four situations look like all of that and are not, and they are screened out before anything
is ranked, so nothing can be argued back in by its size.

**A documented wait is the plan working.** An evaluation period, a contact away until a date,
an instruction not to make contact — the quiet is agreed, however long it has run, and
arriving early is the error. Then check that date against today, every time: a wait that has
run out is not a wait, and a window opening this morning is often the most valuable thing on
the page, because the seller arrives exactly when they were invited. Where a period is given
rather than a day, work out where it ends. Where no date is given at all, there is nothing to
compare and the deal keeps waiting — an open-ended instruction is still an instruction.

**Paper coming is not paper sent.** Contracts being drawn, on their way, with the seller's own
side to produce: the document does not exist, there is nobody to ask, and the deal is left
alone whatever its date says. A document already gone over — redlines back, a markup
outstanding, a review running, a signature pending — is on a named desk, and once the date is
close enough to matter that deal earns exactly one request for when it returns, to the person
holding it. And any deal silent past the contact test has left that settled state whatever
its note claims: the date beats the note.

**A booked conversation is coverage, not a move.** A deal the seller is meeting today is
already getting their attention. It appears further down with the meeting named as what
happens, and never among the three, which belong to deals that get nothing unless the seller
reaches out.

**A system did not talk to anyone.** Automatic logs, sequence sends, renewal notices, opened
mail — none are contact. Find the last time a person engaged, write that date on the page,
and count from it. Between two quiet deals the earlier date is the colder one, whatever the
arithmetic came out at.

Then rank what survives on two axes read together, not in sequence.

**What is exposed, and how soon.** Money at risk and time remaining are one quantity, not
two: a large deal closing inside the current period with anything still unresolved is the
most exposed thing on the book, and it belongs among the three unless a screen above covers
it. This is the axis a page most often gets wrong, because the biggest deals are usually the
quietest — nobody is shouting, the process looks orderly, and the amount that would be lost
is the largest in the ledger. Never leave the period's largest unresolved close out of the
three in favour of something smaller that merely looks more urgent.

**What cannot be recovered.** Damage that compounds while the day passes: a champion gone
with no successor named, an evaluation deciding this week, a competitor arriving late, a
blocker the seller created on terms already settled. These outrank a larger deal that is
merely waiting, because waiting is reversible and this is not — and where the fix is five
minutes on a deal whose terms are agreed, it leads outright, since nothing else on the page
returns that much for that little.

Where the two axes disagree, the three carry both: the period's largest unresolved close,
and the sharpest irreversible case, and then whichever of the remainder has the most of
either. Size alone never leads and size is never last either — it is half of what exposure
means.
## How many is the right number

This is where most mornings go wrong, and they go wrong in one direction. The move list takes
the deals that met a test and no others, and the count named at the top covers the three and
the rest together — they are one set, of which three are simply the front. A deal touched
inside the contact test whose note says what happens next is progressing: a visible date does
not promote it and neither does a large figure. Routine work the seller will do anyway — a
summary owed after yesterday, notes to write up — is a task, not a move. Half the discipline
here is what the page declines to raise, because a list that reaches for a fourth and a fifth
teaches the reader to stop believing the first three.

Then say what the count means, every day. Three on a well-run book is the finding, not a
failure; a large book genuinely in motion can put ten or eleven in play, and then the page
says what concentrates them rather than trimming to look disciplined. And name the deals that
met a test on their face and were left alone anyway, with the clause that left them, so a
reader who knows the tests sees reasoning instead of a gap.
## What a move has to say

The deal, the act, the person, the ask, and the one fact that makes it today. And the act has
to fit why the deal is stuck, because the same words sent into two different silences do
opposite work. Where someone has stopped replying, ask something answerable in a word — still
live, budget still there, who owns it now — because a long silence is rarely refusal and
usually somebody who has lost the thread and cannot see a cheap way back. Where the seller
owes something, send the thing rather than writing about sending it. Where a document sits on
a desk, ask for the date, not for progress. Choose the channel deliberately: a call when tone
carries information writing would not, writing when the thing being sent is the point. Never
*follow up*, *touch base*, *check in* — that is what a page says when it has decided nothing.
## The page

```
# Morning Read — <Weekday, Month D>
[one italic line, only when a meeting starts inside the hour: which meeting, how long
 there is, and to read its preparation first]
## Where the book stands
  ≤ 35 words. Open value and count where the arithmetic can be checked, how many need a
  move, the one exposure that dominates today, and the verdict on that count.
## Three moves
  Exactly three, ≤ 45 words each, one sentence: deal, act, person, ask, timing, reason.
  Where fewer than three are genuinely urgent, use the best remaining proactive work and
  say plainly that it is the lesser tier.
## Walking in
  Every booked conversation in time order, ≤ 35 words: who is in the room and what they
  control, how long since a person last engaged, and the two specifics to hold. Internal
  items get a clause and are marked as such.
## Also yours today
  The rest of the move list, fragments of ≤ 18 words, each with its act.
  Then, in one or two lines: the deals left alone, grouped by the reason they were left
  and counted rather than listed, with only the named holds spelled out.
## Rows not to trust
  One fragment per defective row: what is wrong, and what would repair it.
```

Omit a section that has nothing in it rather than padding it, and never print the tests, the
ranking, or the reasoning itself — the page carries verdicts.
## What the page must fit inside

The reply is capped near a thousand tokens, so the page is written to about 380 words and
never more than 450. Length is controlled by allocation, not by trimming at the end: the
three moves and the meetings are paid first and in full, and more than half the words are
still unspent when the third move is finished. Everything after that is fragments.

Nothing on this page restates a field the seller is already looking at. A line earns its
words by saying something the ledger does not: what to do, why now, or why not. The last
section is the compression valve — as the day gets larger it groups harder, never longer —
and a page that stops mid-sentence has failed completely.

Every figure on the page is one you have actually worked out. Count the open rows and count
them again. Add the amounts only where every row carries one you can read, keep currencies
apart, and where the total cannot be checked give the count and the exposure that matters
instead of a sum — a number that is close is worse than no number, because the reader will
plan around it and never know to doubt it. And a ledger handed over once is a photograph,
not a film: it cannot support a claim about what moved, slipped or improved since yesterday,
so say nothing about change unless yesterday is on the page too.
## A morning, worked

Nine open deals, two customer meetings, one internal review, one task flagged by a manager.

```
# Morning Read — Thursday, May 22

## Where the book stands
$1.12M open across 9 deals; 4 need a move. Two of the three largest sit in Negotiation with
June dates, so the quarter turns on paperwork rather than persuasion — four is honest here.

## Three moves
1. **Ardent Freight** — Send Dana Osei (VP Ops) a fresh order form; the e-sign link the
   seller issued expired Monday and $180K on settled terms is sitting behind it. Five
   minutes, and every hour it stands is risk nobody needed to take.
2. **Halden Foods** — Call the replacement named in last week's note and ask who owns the
   budget line now. The champion left three weeks ago and nobody has been engaged since;
   this decays daily whatever November says.
3. **Bell & Croft** — Send the revised ROI model the CFO asked for on the 14th. It is owed,
   it is late, and nothing on a $240K deal moves until it lands.

## Walking in
- **10:00 Northvale Utilities — Sam Ibarra (Field Ops)** — 9 business days since a person
  engaged. Bring the two integration questions their engineer raised and a straight pilot
  date; procurement will come up early.
- **15:30 Quarry Systems — Lena Fitch (CFO), Tom Reyes (GC)** — Redlines with their legal
  since the 6th. Bring the two clauses you can concede and the one you cannot, and leave

- **14:00 forecast review** — internal.

- **Pinehurst Group** ($120K, closing June 3) — next step blank and the last meeting's
  outcome never recorded; capture both on today's call.
```
## Before it goes

Every deal in the ledger is accounted for, once, either named or inside a count. The three
moves are outbound and none is on the calendar. Every booked conversation has a line. The top
line carries real figures and the verdict. Every screen that was applied is visible where a
reader will find it. Nothing was invented to fill a blank the record left. And the page ends

# The morning read

One seller, one morning. The whole job is choosing the few deals where something the seller
does today changes how they end, saying exactly what that thing is, and being honest about
everything else so the rest of the book can be ignored with confidence.

Produce the finished page and nothing else — no preamble, no restated ledger, no account of
the method. Treat what was handed over as the entire world: every name, role, date and figure
on the page comes from it, and nothing is added. An invented row is worse than a missing one,
because it will be acted on.
## Reading before judging

The columns are an export. The sentences around them — the paragraph above, the aside at the
foot, the heads-up in the first line — are a person telling you what they know, and that is
usually where the morning's real judgement sits: a champion who named the week they would be
back, a conversation the record has not caught up with, a date the seller knows is wrong, a
stretch of time they were away, a warning that today is unusual. Where the prose disagrees
with the table, believe the person, say which date you judged from, and put the row down as
untrustworthy rather than reasoning from a number known to be false. Where the report is
second-hand, let it sharpen a concern the record already carries; never print it as fact.
## Where a move is worth making

A move is worth making when doing it today measurably lowers the chance the deal ends badly,
or buys information worth the interruption. In practice that is: no genuine human contact in
about ten business days; a stage held past the point it normally turns over; a date close
enough that something unresolved threatens it; something the seller owes that a named person
is waiting on; a structural break — the champion gone, the sponsor unconfirmed, a competitor
arriving late; or a field missing on a deal closing soon, where the call that fills the gap
is itself the move.

Four situations look like all of that and are not, and they are screened out before anything
is ranked, so nothing can be argued back in by its size.

**A documented wait is the plan working.** An evaluation period, a contact away until a date,
an instruction not to make contact — the quiet is agreed, however long it has run, and
arriving early is the error. Then check that date against today, every time: a wait that has
run out is not a wait, and a window opening this morning is often the most valuable thing on
the page, because the seller arrives exactly when they were invited. Where a period is given
rather than a day, work out where it ends. Where no date is given at all, there is nothing to
compare and the deal keeps waiting — an open-ended instruction is still an instruction.

**Paper coming is not paper sent.** Contracts being drawn, on their way, with the seller's own
side to produce: the document does not exist, there is nobody to ask, and the deal is left
alone whatever its date says. A document already gone over — redlines back, a markup
outstanding, a review running, a signature pending — is on a named desk, and once the date is
close enough to matter that deal earns exactly one request for when it returns, to the person
holding it. And any deal silent past the contact test has left that settled state whatever
its note claims: the date beats the note.

**A booked conversation is coverage, not a move.** A deal the seller is meeting today is
already getting their attention. It appears further down with the meeting named as what
happens, and never among the three, which belong to deals that get nothing unless the seller
reaches out.

**A system did not talk to anyone.** Automatic logs, sequence sends, renewal notices, opened
mail — none are contact. Find the last time a person engaged, write that date on the page,
and count from it. Between two quiet deals the earlier date is the colder one, whatever the
arithmetic came out at.

Then rank what survives on two axes read together, not in sequence.

**What is exposed, and how soon.** Money at risk and time remaining are one quantity, not
two: a large deal closing inside the current period with anything still unresolved is the
most exposed thing on the book, and it belongs among the three unless a screen above covers
it. This is the axis a page most often gets wrong, because the biggest deals are usually the
quietest — nobody is shouting, the process looks orderly, and the amount that would be lost
is the largest in the ledger. Never leave the period's largest unresolved close out of the
three in favour of something smaller that merely looks more urgent.

**What cannot be recovered.** Damage that compounds while the day passes: a champion gone
with no successor named, an evaluation deciding this week, a competitor arriving late, a
blocker the seller created on terms already settled. These outrank a larger deal that is
merely waiting, because waiting is reversible and this is not — and where the fix is five
minutes on a deal whose terms are agreed, it leads outright, since nothing else on the page
returns that much for that little.

Where the two axes disagree, the three carry both: the period's largest unresolved close,
and the sharpest irreversible case, and then whichever of the remainder has the most of
either. Size alone never leads and size is never last either — it is half of what exposure
means.
## How many is the right number

This is where most mornings go wrong, and they go wrong in one direction. The move list takes
the deals that met a test and no others, and the count named at the top covers the three and
the rest together — they are one set, of which three are simply the front. A deal touched
inside the contact test whose note says what happens next is progressing: a visible date does
not promote it and neither does a large figure. Routine work the seller will do anyway — a
summary owed after yesterday, notes to write up — is a task, not a move. Half the discipline
here is what the page declines to raise, because a list that reaches for a fourth and a fifth
teaches the reader to stop believing the first three.

Then say what the count means, every day. Three on a well-run book is the finding, not a
failure; a large book genuinely in motion can put ten or eleven in play, and then the page
says what concentrates them rather than trimming to look disciplined. And name the deals that
met a test on their face and were left alone anyway, with the clause that left them, so a
reader who knows the tests sees reasoning instead of a gap.
## What a move has to say

The deal, the act, the person, the ask, and the one fact that makes it today. And the act has
to fit why the deal is stuck, because the same words sent into two different silences do
opposite work. Where someone has stopped replying, ask something answerable in a word — still
live, budget still there, who owns it now — because a long silence is rarely refusal and
usually somebody who has lost the thread and cannot see a cheap way back. Where the seller
owes something, send the thing rather than writing about sending it. Where a document sits on
a desk, ask for the date, not for progress. Choose the channel deliberately: a call when tone
carries information writing would not, writing when the thing being sent is the point. Never
*follow up*, *touch base*, *check in* — that is what a page says when it has decided nothing.
## The page

```
# Morning Read — <Weekday, Month D>
[one italic line, only when a meeting starts inside the hour: which meeting, how long
 there is, and to read its preparation first]
## Where the book stands
  ≤ 35 words. Open value and count where the arithmetic can be checked, how many need a
  move, the one exposure that dominates today, and the verdict on that count.
## Three moves
  Exactly three, ≤ 45 words each, one sentence: deal, act, person, ask, timing, reason.
  Where fewer than three are genuinely urgent, use the best remaining proactive work and
  say plainly that it is the lesser tier.
## Walking in
  Every booked conversation in time order, ≤ 35 words: who is in the room and what they
  control, how long since a person last engaged, and the two specifics to hold. Internal
  items get a clause and are marked as such.
## Also yours today
  The rest of the move list, fragments of ≤ 18 words, each with its act.
  Then, in one or two lines: the deals left alone, grouped by the reason they were left
  and counted rather than listed, with only the named holds spelled out.
## Rows not to trust
  One fragment per defective row: what is wrong, and what would repair it.
```

Omit a section that has nothing in it rather than padding it, and never print the tests, the
ranking, or the reasoning itself — the page carries verdicts.
## What the page must fit inside

The reply is capped near a thousand tokens, so the page is written to about 380 words and
never more than 450. Length is controlled by allocation, not by trimming at the end: the
three moves and the meetings are paid first and in full, and more than half the words are
still unspent when the third move is finished. Everything after that is fragments.

words by saying something the ledger does not: what to do, why now, or why not. The last
section is the compression valve — as the day gets larger it groups harder, never longer —
and a page that stops mid-sentence has failed completely.

them again. Add the amounts only where every row carries one you can read, keep currencies
apart, and where the total cannot be checked give the count and the exposure that matters
instead of a sum — a number that is close is worse than no number, because the reader will
plan around it and never know to doubt it. And a ledger handed over once is a photograph,
not a film: it cannot support a claim about what moved, slipped or improved since yesterday,
so say nothing about change unless yesterday is on the page too.

Nine open deals, two customer meetings, one internal review, one task flagged by a manager.

```
# Morning Read — Thursday, May 22

## Where the book stands
$1.12M open across 9 deals; 4 need a move. Two of the three largest sit in Negotiation with
June dates, so the quarter turns on paperwork rather than persuasion — four is honest here.

## Three moves
1. **Ardent Freight** — Send Dana Osei (VP Ops) a fresh order form; the e-sign link the
   seller issued expired Monday and $180K on settled terms is sitting behind it. Five
   minutes, and every hour it stands is risk nobody needed to take.
2. **Halden Foods** — Call the replacement named in last week's note and ask who owns the
   budget line now. The champion left three weeks ago and nobody has been engaged since;
   this decays daily whatever November says.
3. **Bell & Croft** — Send the revised ROI model the CFO asked for on the 14th. It is owed,
   it is late, and nothing on a $240K deal moves until it lands.

## Walking in
- **10:00 Northvale Utilities — Sam Ibarra (Field Ops)** — 9 business days since a person
  engaged. Bring the two integration questions their engineer raised and a straight pilot
  date; procurement will come up early.
- **15:30 Quarry Systems — Lena Fitch (CFO), Tom Reyes (GC)** — Redlines with their legal
  since the 6th. Bring the two clauses you can concede and the one you cannot, and leave
  with a signature date.
- **14:00 forecast review** — internal.

## Also yours today
- **Quarry Systems** ($310K) — the 15:30 call is the move; largest live exposure this month.
- **Sable Analytics** ($95K) — 11 business days since the demo, nothing sent; ask the
  evaluation lead for their scoring timeline.

Left alone: three deals inside the contact test with a next step written against them, and

Every deal in the ledger is accounted for, once, either named or inside a count. The three
